abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: Opioid consumption is associated with various risks to pregnancies in humans and mice. Here, we have used single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis to determine how exposure to pharmacologically relevant levels of opioid drug oxycodone (OXY) affects different mouse placenta cell lineages. These placental cells include parietal trophoblast giant cells (pTGC), large secretory cells that participate in controlling maternal metabolism to accommodate the pregnancy, as well in the placenta–brain axis of the developing fetus. The pTGC have eluded previous attempts to characterize their transcriptome profile beyond the initial stages of pregnancy. OXY exposure caused extensive loss of pTGC and transcriptomic changes indicative of stress throughout the junctional zone of the placenta that borders maternal uterine tissue.

Pregnant women are often prescribed or abuse opioid drugs. The placenta is likely the key to understanding how opioids cause adverse pregnancy outcomes. Maternal oxycodone (OXY) exposure of pregnant mice leads to disturbances in the layer of invasive parietal trophoblast giant cells (pTGC) that forms the interface between the placenta and uterus. These cells are analogous to extravillous trophoblasts of the human placenta. They are crucial to coordinating the metabolic needs of the conceptus with those of the mother and are primary participants in the placenta–brain axis. Their large nuclear size, however, has precluded both single-cell (sc) and single-nucleus (sn) RNA-seq analyses beyond embryonic day (E) 8.5. Here, we compared the transcriptomes of placentas from pregnant mice exposed to OXY with unexposed controls at E12.5, with particular emphasis on the pTGC. The nonfluidic Parse snRNA-seq approach permitted characterization of the nuclear transcriptomes of all the major placental cell lineages and their presumed progenitors at E12.5. OXY exposure had a negligible effect on components of the placental labyrinth, including the two syncytial cell layers, but caused transcriptomic changes consistent with metabolic stress throughout the spongiotrophoblast. Most notably, there was loss of the majority of pTGC, whose normal gene expression is consistent with elevated energy demand relating to biosynthesis of multiple secretory products, especially hormones, and endoduplication of DNA. This unusual sensitivity of pTGC presumably puts the pregnancy and future health of the offspring at particular risk to OXY exposure.

body.p: The opioid crisis is a leading noncommunicable disease plaguing many communities. Additionally, opioid drugs are often used to control pain during pregnancy, and pregnant women can become addicted to such drugs, while others abuse them. As a result, infants prenatally exposed to opioids are at risk for neonatal abstinence syndrome and other outcomes associated with maternal opioid use disorder, including poor fetal growth, low birth weight, and premature birth (1, 2). The long-term effects on such children remain uncertain, although, in the mouse, long-term behavioral defects have been noted (3).

The mouse and human placentas have opioid signaling pathways that have been suggested to be integral in regulating the production of placental hormones (4–8). Maternal opioid treatment likely disturbs such processes. Only a handful of studies, however, have examined how opioids alter placental function or individual trophoblast (TB) cell lineage development and performance (9–12). OXY acts through endogenous opioid receptors expressed in human and mouse TB (13–18) and, in so doing, probably disturbs normal endogenous opioid-mediated actions that regulate production of key placental proteins in the human, such as chorionic gonadotropin (CG) and placental lactogen (5–7, 19, 20). Opioids also affect calcium signaling, acetylcholine release, and aromatase conversion of testosterone to estrogen within the human placenta (21–23). Chronic consumption of another opioid drug, methadone, blunts the actions of opioid receptors in human placental villous tissue (24), leading to opioid tolerance by suppressing kappa opioid receptors and accompanying downstream signaling pathways (25). The use of methadone and a related drug used for opioid dependence, buprenorphine, correlates with a variety of increased placental developmental abnormalities (26). Analogous findings of delayed villous maturation in pregnant women exposed to opioids have been reported (11). Morphine administration to pregnant mothers significantly correlates with vasoconstriction of placental vasculature, thereby compromising nutrient and oxygen delivery to the fetus (27). One of us has summarized placental opioid effects in a recent review (28).

Much though remains to be determined as to how OXY acts in the placenta. Previously, we examined how maternal exposure to OXY affects the mouse placenta, which shares many common features with the human (29–31). Females were exposed to a physiologically relevant dose of OXY two weeks prior to breeding (periconceptional period) and up until the time the placentas were collected at embryonic age (E) 9.5 and 12.5, a period that we, and others, have shown to be highly sensitive to environmental insults (29, 32–35). As noted previously, when studying the effects of endocrine-disrupting chemicals, the large secondary parietal trophoblast giant cells (pTGC) at the interface between the placental spongiotrophoblast layer and the maternal decidual tissues appeared to be targeted (36–38). Maternal OXY treatment reduced the area occupied by pTGC and decreased the maternal blood vessel area within the labyrinth region (39). Like human extravillous trophoblast cells, the pTGC are at the interface of the fetal placenta and maternal uterine tissue and exert critical roles in modulating maternal metabolism to meet the needs of the fetus. They are also postulated to be primary participants in the placenta–brain axis and supply serotonin to the emerging brain (31, 32, 40, 41).

To help sort out the TB-specific effects, single-nuclei or single-cell RNA (snRNA-seq and scRNA-seq) sequencing approaches are needed. However, sizes of the pTGG and their constituent nuclei are obstacles to such transcriptomic analyses and place a limitation on the data that can be obtained (42, 43). One study that used the 10X Genomics scRNA-seq approach revealed a cluster of cells with pTGC marker genes at E 8.5 but not thereafter when the pTGC have become larger (44). To overcome this obstacle, we opted to use the recently developed Parse Biosciences protocol that uses split-pool combinatorial barcoding to provide nuclear transcripts within each nucleus a unique identifying nucleotide tag before further processing (45). We used this method to identify different lineages of placental trophoblast, including pTGC, at E12.5 and to examine how OXY exposure affects the placenta. There now appears to be agreement that snRNA-seq and scRNA-seq provide similar outcomes with regard to cell type cluster identification and the transcriptomic profile of the constituent cells, despite the fact that the majority of nuclear transcripts are not fully processed to mature mRNA (46).

sec.title: General Features of Pregnant Mice and snRNA-seq Analysis of E12.5 Placentas.
sec.p: No overt differences were detected in the mice at the time of breeding/plug formation and when placentas were collected at E 12.5 (SI Appendix, Fig. S1). No differences in litter sizes were found. SI Appendix, Table S1 includes the samples analyzed and the Evercode WT Barcoding Plate Configuration. SI Appendix, Table S2 provides the total number of reads, nuclei, and identified genes. In total, 4,522 nuclei underwent analysis. Total reads were 298,389,746, of which 75.0 % could be mapped to reference genome GRCm38. The total genes identified were 28,436. At this stage of the analysis, it became clear that one replicate of the OXY placenta (A1) and one in the saline CTL placenta (A11) provided anomalous data and were removed (these are highlighted in SI Appendix, Table S2). In each, the number of recovered nuclei was few, and preliminary UMAP analysis revealed that these nuclei largely distributed into a unique cluster to which the other placental/decidual samples did not contribute.

sec.title: Cluster Distribution of E12.5 Nuclei.
sec.p: The Seurat program distributed the E 12.5 nuclei into 16 (0 to 15) (Fig. 1A) clusters. While the dissected placental samples were predominantly from the conceptus, they also contained decidual tissue. By contrast, decidual tissue was expected to be largely free of contaminating placenta except possibly for invasive trophoblast cells. Accordingly, it was possible to distinguish placental cells from decidual cells by comparing side-by-side UMAP diagrams (Fig. 1A). We also considered these clusters in relation to whether the placental and decidual tissues were from OXY vs. saline control (CTL) groups, discussed further below (Fig. 1B).

caption.p: Transcript distribution among different clusters of nuclei in the E12.5 fetal placenta and maternal decidua, as determined following snRNA-seq. (A) Distribution of the E12.5 nuclei into 16 (0 to 15) clusters based on Seurat analysis. Decidual and placental tissue were dissected and barcoded separately from each other. This figure shows it is possible to distinguish placental cells from decidual cells by comparing side-by-side UMAP diagrams. (B) The effect of OXY on the distribution of nuclei among the 16 different clusters. (C) Spliced vs. nonspliced transcripts i.e., those containing introns, in the different clusters. Approximately two-thirds of the transcripts in all clusters, except those of Cluster 10 contained introns.

sec.p: On this basis, clusters 0, 3, 12, and possibly 15 were judged to be decidual tissue. However, the lineage origin, i.e., whether decidual or placental, of Cluster 4 is not easily decided from this visual comparison of the two UMAPs (Fig. 1A) and will be discussed later. Approximately two-thirds of the transcripts in all clusters, except those of Cluster 10, contained introns (Fig. 1C), consistent with incomplete processing and a nuclear source. The probable basis for the increased proportion of intron-less transcripts in Cluster 10 is discussed later.

Clusters 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, and 14 were placental. When total transcriptomes were analyzed by the TissueEnrich program (47), all, including Cluster 4, but with the exception of Cluster 14, showed a highly significant resemblance to the E14.5 mouse placenta (SI Appendix, Fig. S2). Cluster 9 had some transcriptomic features in common with other fetal organs (limb, heart, and brain), but the placental phenotype was still dominant. Cluster 14, on the other hand, showed only a weak resemblance to the placenta and a relatively strong link to the liver and kidney.

sec.title: Identification of Specific Cell Types Providing Nuclei to Different Clusters at E12.5.
sec.p: All genes in each cluster, including those differentially expressed, are provided in Dataset S1. The 100-most up-regulated (>2-fold; P < 0.01) genes in all clusters are listed in Dataset S2. Heat maps for the top 100 up-regulated genes for each cluster are shown (SI Appendix, Fig. S3). More information on each of these genes is provided in Dataset S3. Of the sixteen, Clusters 1, 4, and 16 were the least well defined by using this criterion, while Clusters 3, 10, and 11 provided the most consistent displays of up-regulated genes across their constituent nuclei. Known specific markers associated with decidual tissue and individual trophoblast cell types were used to provide a tentative identification of each cluster.

On this basis, Cluster 0, with up-regulated Esr1, Pgr, and Prl8a2, largely represents decidualized stromal cells, and Cluster 3, with up-regulated Ramp3, Clca2, and Lef1, uterine surface and/or glandular epithelial cells. Of the two remaining decidual clusters, Cluster 12 is characterized by upregulation of Rgs1, Runx3, Prf1, and Cd96. The latter encodes an immune checkpoint factor on the surface of T cells (48). This nontrophoblast cluster assumingly represents either a NK- or T cell population resident close to the implantation site, as it appears to be carried over to the placental samples (Fig. 1A). The small Cluster 15, like 3, carries markers expected of uterine epithelium. None of these decidual clusters appear to have been affected in terms of nuclear numbers by OXY exposure (Fig. 1B), although, as discussed later, there were some minor changes in gene expression noted in Clusters 0 and 3.

Cluster 1, as evident from the upregulation of genes such as Hand1, Runx1, Grhl2, and Wnt7b, the guanylate cyclase subunit Gucy1b2, and placenta-specific glycoproteins, such as Psg16, 17, 18, 19, and 28 (Dataset S2 and Fig. 2 A and B) is clearly complex. It likely comprises precursors of various spongioTB lineages, such as pTGC (Cluster 10), among others. Cluster 2 is inferred to be comprised largely of nuclei from glycogen cells, which mainly populate the junctional zone of the mouse placenta at E12.5 (49). Up-regulated markers include Ncam1, Igfbp7, Plac8, Pla3G4e, and Cdhr5 (Dataset S2 and Fig. 2 A and B). Cluster 4 is less well defined than Cluster 2 through its top 100 up-regulated genes (Fig. 2 A and B) but shares several markers in common with Cluster 1 and Cluster 10 (pTGC; see below) and 13. Its nuclei carry markers that demark invasive spiral artery giant cells (SpaGC), for example, Prl7a2, Prl3b1, Ctsq (Dataset S2), Cd36, and Chrdl1 (Fig. 2 A and B). SpaTGC are known to remodel arterial walls and replace maternal endothelial cells relatively deep in the deciduum (50, 51). Therefore, their common presence in decidual as well as placental tissue samples, as inferred from Fig. 1A, is expected.

caption.p: UMAPS of selected markers representing the different clusters of nuclei at E12.5 for placental and decidual tissue. Each of the transcripts is among the top 20 genes in that cluster significantly up-regulated (>4-fold, q < 0.0001) relative to its expression in all other placental clusters). (A) Shows the UMAPS for these select markers. (B) Shows the dot plot for these select markers. The same scale is used for all UMAPS and circles in the dot plot.

sec.p: Cluster 5, which includes genes encoding transcription factors, such as Tox2, and Grhl2 (Fig. 2 A and B) and Hand1, signaling pathway components such as Wnt7b and Ghrh are highly up-regulated, has transcriptome features of spongiotrophoblast, which, along with glycogen cells (Cluster 2), are the major component cell types of the Junctional Zone. Many of the up-regulated genes in Cluster 6 have to do with cellular proliferation (Mki67, Met, and Kif gene family members), cell cycle control, stem cell maintenance (Lgr5), and patterning. We infer that it contains progenitor populations for other lineages. Highly up-regulated marker genes also include Phactr3 and Brca1 (Fig. 2 A and B).

Well-defined Cluster 7 carries multiple markers for endothelial cells and yolk sac endoderm (Dataset S2), but this latter link seems unlikely at E12.5 when the yolk sac barely contacts the chorion and would be unlikely to contaminate the placental tissue (52). Highly up-regulated markers include Gata4 and Pdpn (Fig. 2 A and B), Adora1, and Ddah1 (Dataset S2). However, Cluster 7 nuclei also express markers such as Prl3b1 and Prl7d1, suggesting that they might represent the sinusoidal giant cells that line the blood sinusoid of the placental labyrinth, although the gene Ctsq, which has been considered to be a marker of such cells after E12.5 (53, 54) is down-regulated relative to other clusters.

The nuclei of the two syncytial cell layers of the labyrinth are represented by Clusters 8 (SynTI) and 11 (SynTII), which form well-defined, well-separated groupings on the UMAP (Fig. 1A). Cluster 8 markers include Tulp1 and Plekhd1 (Fig. 2 A and B), as well as Tgfa, Glis1, Stra6, and Syna (the gene encoding syncytin a, considered to be involved in cell fusion, Dataset S1). Cluster 11 (SynTII) carries a very different set of distinguishing markers from Cluster 8, including Gcm1 and Slc6a13 (Fig. 2 A and B), Gcgr (the glucagon receptor), Cebpa, and three genes (Gabrp, Vtcn, and Wfdc2) described in first-trimester human syncytiotrophoblast (55). Interestingly, Synb, often cited as the gene encoding the fusogen for SynTII, was not among the top 1,000 differentially regulated genes of Cluster 11 (Dataset S1). Cluster 9, like Cluster 6 (but with its own distinct transcriptome profile) appears to have features of the labyrinth and is possibly a precursor form of syncytial trophoblast. Transcripts for Tbx5, Gli2 (Fig. 3 A and B), and Cdh2 are prominently up-regulated in Cluster 9.

caption.p: The UMAP and dot plot distributions of nuclei from placental and decidual tissue expressing six of the Cluster 10 up-regulated genes. Prl3b1, Prl7d1, Prl8a9, Prl2c2, and Tpbpa are “classical” pTGC markers, while Cdk8 is associated with endoduplication of DNA. While other clusters (1, 2, 4, and 5) also express each of the classical markers, the average expression and percent of nuclei expressing the transcript are significantly lower than in Cluster 10. (A) Shows the UMAPS for each of these genes. (B) Shows the diet dot plot for these genes. The same scale is used for all UMAPS and circles in the dot plot.

sec.p: Cluster 10 represents pTGC, the major focus of this study. The genes with highest expression and that are more than sevenfold up-regulated in Cluster 10 are listed in Table 1. Among the most prominent of the up-regulated genes associated with cluster 10 are Cair and Pdia3, whose UMAP patterns are illustrated in Fig. 2 A and B), several genes of the prolactin superfamily (including Prl3b1, Prl7d1, and Prl2c2), Tpbpa, and Cdk8 (Fig. 3 A and B), and others, such as Igf2 and Cdk8. In addition, the gene encoding the CDK1 inhibitor Cdkn1c (also known as p57) is also up-regulated in Cluster 10 (Dataset S1). Both Cdk8 and Cdkn1c have been implicated in the extensive endoduplication of the genome of pTGC (56, 57), but are also likely to be expressed in all cells where DNA replication and repair is encountered. Unexpectedly, Prl2c2, which encodes the growth factor proliferin, and is frequently used as a specific histological marker of pTGC (58–61), is not among the top 100 most up-regulated genes of Cluster 10, although it is primarily expressed there (Fig. 3 A and B). The UMAP distributions of nuclei expressing six of the Cluster 10 “markers” indicate that 1) their expression patterns are quite similar but not identical; 2) the expression of each Prl gene extends into Clusters 1, 2, 4, and 5, albeit at lower levels in terms of average expression and percent of nuclei presenting the transcripts than in Cluster 10 (Fig. 3 A and B); 3) The same four genes are also expressed in SpaTGC (Cluster 4). Finally, five of the top 10 most up-regulated genes in Cluster 10 are mitochondrially encoded, namely mt-Nd6, mt-Cytb, mt-Co1, mt-Nd1, and mt-Nd5 (Dataset S2 and SI Appendix, Fig. S4). Based on UMAP figures, these four genes have identical expression patterns, which are quite similar to those of the Cluster 10 markers Prl7d1 and Prl2c2 (Fig. 3 A and B) A total of nine mt-genes are among the top 100 up-regulated genes in Cluster 10 (Dataset S2). Mt-genes do not feature among the top up-regulated genes in any TB cluster but Cluster 10. Most likely mitochondria form a relatively tight association with the nuclei of pTGC and survive the nuclear isolation procedure and the subsequent steps preceding library construction. This same phenomenon appears to have also occurred, but to a lesser extent, during processing of nuclei from the surface and glandular epithelium (Cluster 3) of the uterus (SI Appendix, Fig. S4).

The mt-gene transcripts, which lack introns, account for about 1 % of the total present in Cluster 10 and cannot account fully for why there is a greater proportion of apparently fully processed transcripts in Cluster 10 than in other clusters (Fig. 1C). However, Cluster 10 nuclei are also highly enriched in other transcripts derived from RNA genes, such as MALAT1 and Rn18s-rs5, and there is no evidence for increased processing of protein-encoding transcripts in general (Dataset S4).

Importation of the top 100 genes expressed in Cluster 10 into the PlacentaCellEnrich program (62), which is based on human placenta and associated tissue transcripts, revealed that pTGC align closely with human extravillous trophoblast cells (Fig. 4A), as proposed by others (49, 63, 64). Analysis of the top 100 differentially expressed genes in Cluster 10 with the mammalian phenotype ontology function for the WebGestalt program (65) suggests that anomalous expression of its genes is associated with abnormal placental size and morphology (Fig. 4B).

caption.p: Analyses of the top 100 differentially expressed genes in Cluster 10 by the PlacentaCellEnrich, and WebGestalt programs to examine for phenotypes and diseases associated with these transcripts. (A) The PlacentaCellEnrich program (62), which is based on the human placenta and associated tissue transcripts, revealed that these cells most closely align to human extravillous trophoblast cells. (B) The WebGestalt program (65) suggests that disturbances in the expression of these genes are associated with abnormal placental size and morphology.

sec.p: Cluster 13, with strong signatures of TB (SI Appendix, Fig. S2), displays Zfp366, often used to identify dendritic cells (66) (Fig. 2), plus several macrophage and monocyte markers (Cd36, Cd34, and Meox2). This cluster appears to represent a scavenging cell population of some kind. Its markers display considerable overlap with Cluster 4 (SpaTGC) nuclei (Fig. 2). Finally, Cluster 14 is marked by the marked upregulation of many genes associated with stress and vascular dysfunction (Prodh2), fetal drug exposure and toxicity (Abcc2, Abcc6, and Slca9), metal toxicity (Atp7b) and hypoxia (Agt), as well as complement family members. Few diagnostic TB cell markers are associated with this cluster, although there is weak expression of a few genes with characteristics of trophoblast (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 and Dataset S2).

The top 100 genes in each cluster were imported into the WEB-based GEne SeT AnaLysis Toolkit (WebGestalt) 2019 version to search for gene ontology molecular function (GO MF) and gene ontology biological processes (GO BP) (65). Fig. 5 shows the GO terms enriched with Clusters 1, 5, 10, which, as discussed later, are of primary interest with regard to OXY effects. Primary GO terms associated with Cluster 1 include syncytium formation, multicellular organism processes, and multiorganism reproductive processes. Those associated with Cluster 5 include placenta development and development growth involved in morphogenesis. GO terms associated with Cluster 10 also include placenta development but also ameboidal-type cell migration, wound healing, protein maturation, and response to endoplasmic reticulum stress. The GO terms for the remaining clusters (see SI Appendix, Fig. S5) are generally consistent with their inferred identities, e.g., Cluster 7 has enrichment of endoderm development, while Cluster 11 displays terms associated with transport and Cluster 14 with xenobiotic stimulus.

caption.p: The top 100 genes in each cluster were imported into the WEB-based GEne SeT AnaLysis Toolkit (WebGestalt) 2019 version to search for gene ontology molecular function (GO MF) and gene ontology biological processes (GO BP) (65) enriched for clusters 1, 5, and 10.

sec.title: Effects of Oxycodone on Cluster Makeup at E12.5.
sec.p: Upon examination of the E12.5 UMAPs, it was evident that OXY exposure of the dams led to changes in the distribution of nuclei across placental clusters (Fig. 1B). There was no discernible influence, however, on any of the decidual clusters (0, 3, 12, and 15). The most marked consequence of OXY on placental TB was the almost complete loss of pTGC nuclei, i.e., Cluster 10, and a relative reduction of nuclei in the part of Cluster 1 that forms a bridge to Cluster 10 in control placentas. This region of Cluster 1 expresses many of the markers associated with Cluster 10 and is presumed to contain pTGC and SpaTGC precursors (Figs. 2 and 3). There was also some apparent OXY-associated loss of nuclei in the central and lower region of Cluster 2 (glycogen cells). Together, these observations suggest that OXY effects are largely directed at the junctional zone of the mouse placenta and its interface with the deciduum, with pTGC being the main susceptible cell type. However, the SpaTGC (Cluster 4), although proposed as related to pTGC (49, 67), do not appear to be reduced in number after OXY exposure. No obvious changes were evident in the two syncytial layers STI and STII (Clusters 8 and 11, respectively), nor in clusters inferred to be possible contributors to the labyrinth layer (Clusters 6 and 9).

There was a major gain of nuclei in cluster 14 in the OXY placentas. Indeed Cluster 14 barely exists in the control tissues. As pointed out above, the genes that define Cluster 14 are ones typically up-regulated in response to stressors, especially xenobiotics. The cells comprising this cluster are difficult to define, as they possess a transcriptome that more resembles liver than placental trophoblast (SI Appendix, Fig. S2). Nonetheless, nuclei in Cluster 14 do express several mouse TB markers such as Tpbpa and Prl3b1, albeit weakly (Fig. 3 and Dataset S1).

sec.title: Transcripts Regulated by OXY Exposure: Placental Clusters.
sec.p: Clusters 1 and 10 are the apparent main targets for OXY in terms of nuclear depletion, with Clusters 2 and 5 also possibly affected. However, the paucity of nuclei in Cluster 10 after exposure to OXY precluded a reliable assessment of effects on most genes, Nonetheless, six (Afp, Apob, Ccdc120, Fam20c, Apoe, Rgs20, and Spp2) had become up-regulated (q < 0.05) and highly expressed in the remaining few nuclei of Cluster 10 of the OXY-exposed samples (Dataset S5). On the other hand, the number of OXY-responsive DEGs with q values < 0.05) in Cluster 1 numbers 174, with over 107 displaying adjusted P values (q) < 0.005, Dataset S5). Of the latter about one-third are up-regulated. Strikingly, the top up-regulated genes include at least three (Afp, Apob, and Apoa1) associated with sterol and lipoprotein transport and uptake and are also noted to be linked to the acute phase response and placental stress (68, 69). As well as the above three genes, others are involved in metabolism of vitamins, including retinoids (Gpc3 and Ttr). Most of the same up-regulated genes are noted in Cluster 2 (105 DEGs) and Cluster 5 (28 DEGs) after OXY exposure (Dataset S5). Far fewer DEGs are found in the remaining placental clusters. For example, Cluster 4 displays none, and Cluster 8 (SynTI) and Cluster 11 (SynTII) only six and three, respectively. One up-regulated gene common to all TB clusters affected by OXY is Cwc22, which participates in mRNA binding by the spliceosome complex. Down-regulated genes comprise the majority of DEGs in both Clusters 1 and 2, and, again, many of these are common to both (Dataset S5). They are associated with a wide range of cellular processes, including mRNA processing and splicing.

One additional observation is that most of the up-regulated genes are expressed in only a minority of the nuclei in the control samples, whereas OXY exposure induces their expression in a high proportion of nuclei (Dataset S5). One case in point is Apob, whose expression is detectable in only 5.8 % of Cluster 1 nuclei in control samples, whereas OXY exposure raises this number to 59.3 %. Another more extreme example is Moab (encoding monoamine oxidase b), a gene barely expressed in control nuclei of Cluster 1 (0.9 %) yet up-regulated in 26.9 % of nuclei from OXY-exposed cells. By contrast, the down-regulated genes, for example, Rlim, Lars2, Cdk8, and Gphn, are expressed in a high percentage of both control and OXY-exposed nuclei, although at lower levels in the latter. What these observations imply is unclear.

An examination of two (Prl2c2 and Prl7a1) of the several Prl family members that are marker genes of Cluster 10 illustrates the typical responses observed in OXY-exposed placental tissue (Fig. 6). Nuclei highly positive (intense blue signals) become depleted in Cluster 10, but the few that remain do not appear to have a reduced intensity. The loss of positive nuclei for each marker is also evident in the region that connects Cluster 1 nuclei with Cluster 10. Other non-Prl markers of Cluster 10, such as Hand1 (Fig. 6), a key transcription factor in specifying pTGC (70, 71) provide further confirmatory data for nuclear loss rather than diminished gene expression in these regions. Importantly, none of these genes are among those significantly down- or up-regulated by OXY exposure in either Cluster 1 or 10 (Dataset S5), consistent with the inference that it is primarily loss of cells rather than transcriptional changes that are responsible for declines in expression. Finally, as stated earlier, there is no evidence from the UMAP diagrams for a loss of cells from Cluster 4, the SpaTGC, which may be derived from the same lineage as pTGC (49) but are closely associated with maternal blood vessels within the endometrium. On the other hand, Cluster 14, which is only evident in OXY-exposed tissues, possesses nuclei positive for Prl2c2, Prl7a1, and Hand1, raising the possibility that it represents nuclei from either affected Cluster 10 cells or Cluster 10 progenitor populations.

caption.p: UMAPS for selected genes differentially expressed in the different clusters based on OXY vs. CTL placental samples. An examination of two (Prl8a9 and Prl2c2) of the several of Prl family members that are marker genes of Cluster 10 is illustrative of changes in gene expression in response to OXY.

sec.p: We were not able to confirm whether OXY had a sexually dimorphic effect on gene expression as noted in an earlier publication (39), because each sample analyzed was from pooled placentas. However, several Y-linked genes did show expression changes in response to OXY (SI Appendix, Table S3). Thus, we have confirmed the presence of male tissues in the included samples but cannot drawn definitive conclusions on sex effects. Most of the Y-linked genes were modestly down-regulated by OXY exposure, although there was one exception, Gm29566, whose mean expression in the three control samples was extremely low.

sec.title: Transcripts Regulated by OXY Exposure: Decidual Clusters.
sec.p: Dataset S5 also provides values for effects of OXY on gene expression in maternal clusters 0 and 3. Relatively few genes were affected (31 in Cluster 0; 12 in Cluster 3), and many of the differentially regulated genes were identical in both clusters, including the top three, Camk1d, Cdk8, and Il31ra. In both Clusters 0 and 3, most of the affected genes were down-regulated, but some, for example, Atn1 (encoding atrophin), a transcriptional corepressor, and Mbd6, encoding a methyl-CpG binding protein, were up-regulated (each approximately fourfold in Cluster 3; Dataset S5). The number of nuclei in the remaining decidual clusters (12, 13, and 15) was too small to make a meaningful analysis of gene expression changes.

sec.title: Expression of Opioid Receptor Genes.
sec.p: Although there have been reports that genes for some opioid receptors are expressed in the mouse and human placenta (14, 17, 28), including the delta-receptor (Oprd1) in pTGC (17), our sequencing data indicate that only one (Oprm1) is expressed at E12.5 (Dataset S1) and then only in Clusters 1, 5, and 14. Expression was generally low, although a few nuclei reveal more intense expression (SI Appendix, Fig. S6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The mouse and human placenta are composed of a complex mixture of TB cell types. The pTGC exhibit parallels to human extravillous trophoblast cells as they are at the interface of the fetal placenta and maternal uterine tissue, which places them in an ideal location for modulating the dialogue between the dam and conceptus. Such cells play important contributory roles in the placenta–brain axis by providing serotonin and likely other bioactive molecules to the developing brain (31, 32, 40, 41). However, secondary pTGC from maturing mouse placentas, have eluded most conventional approaches of sn- and scRNA-seq analysis (42–44), although there is one report of bulk analysis of the transcriptome of pTGC that had been loosened from hand-dissected placentas at E9.5 (56). The secondary pTGC are not only large but their DNA undergoes extensive endoreplication as the cells mature, such that their nuclei are generally more than 50 μm in diameter, sometimes exceeding 100 μm, which is beyond the upper limit (~40 µm) possible with the standard filtration and microfluidics processing of the 10X Genomics sequencing platform. In addition, scRNA-seq, unlike snRNA-seq, fails to provide adequate information on syncytiotrophoblast, where cells have fused to form large fragile structures. Jiang et al. (72) used standard 10X Genomics scRNA-seq to provide a comprehensive accounting of TB cell types from E7.5 to E14.5. They reported the transcriptomes of SynTI and SynTII precursors, but not those of the mature, presumably fully syncytialized cells. They also reported success for populations of secondary pTGC and their precursors early in pregnancy (E8.5) when pTGC are initially forming and not exceeding the theoretical 40 µm cutoff. By E12.5, pTGC and their nuclei are much larger and would almost certainly have been excluded from any single-cell libraries. Marsh and Blelloch (42) used snRNA-seq and were able to follow the formation of the labyrinth and its two STB components, but failed to obtain data on pTGC, again presumably because of the limitation imposed by nuclear size (49, 67, 73–75).

To overcome this size hurdle, we chose a nonmicrofluidic approach (45) to determine the transcriptome profile of pTGC in the mouse placenta at E12.5. In this procedure, the isolated nuclei are fixed, distributed into wells, and a sample-specific barcode added to transcripts in situ by a reverse transcription reaction. The nuclei from all samples are then mixed into one pool and redistributed across a new set of wells before adding a second unique barcode to each sample. After repeating this procedure a third time, the pooled nuclei are again redistributed into new wells, lysed, a fourth barcode added, and library construction performed. This process avoids the need to capture individual nuclei for library construction, while the four rounds of split pool barcoding are sufficient to provide a unique tag to each nucleus.

The Parse protocol provided 16 clusters of nuclei (Fig. 1), some well-defined, others less so, originating from the placenta, although the use of shear forces and multiple filtration and centrifugation steps to release nuclei would undoubtedly have influenced the final cluster yields. Of these 16 clusters, Cluster 10 represents secondary pTGC. These cells are distinct from the primary pTGC, which form from mural trophectoderm at the initiation of implantation. Instead, the secondary pTGC originate from cells occupying the distal end of the ectoplacental cone as the true placenta begins to form around E8.5. The transcriptome of the cluster 10 nuclei is consistent with earlier immunohistochemical studies and the bulk RNA-seq analysis of Sher et al. (56) that these cells are highly secretory, phagocytic, and invasive as well as having an endocrine role, which includes the production of proliferin (PRL2C2/PLF a prolactin-related protein) (76, 77) and mouse placental lactogen 1 (PRL3D1) and II (PRL3B1), as well as IGF2, all of which are believed to assist in modulating maternal physiology to benefit the needs of the growing conceptus. Clearly, any compound that impinges on pTCG activities would likely influence this fetal–maternal dialog and negatively affect the placenta (Fig. 4B) and pregnancy. Yet, the effects of OXY, although quite dramatic in terms of placental phenotype and the loss of a prominent cell type, appear to have relatively subtle consequences on pregnancy outcomes in these optimally maintained laboratory mice, but they go on to have gut microbiome and behavioral changes (3, 78). Conceivably, more environmentally challenging conditions would result in less propitious outcomes, as noted following the genetic ablation of a single Prl gene, Prl4a1 (79). Prl4a1 is expressed prominently in pTGC (Table 1), but its loss provides no discernible phenotype in mice kept in a vivarium. However, loss of function is lethal around mid-pregnancy under mildly hypobaric conditions.

Not only are the pTGC involved in intense biosynthetic activities, another feature of these cells that must contribute to unusual energy demand is the massive endoduplication of their chromosomal DNA (56, 75). Possibly linked to this need for ATP and reducing power is another feature of Cluster 10, namely the high level of transcripts originating from mitochondria. To explain this phenomenon, we suggest that the nuclei from pTGC carried with them adhering mitochondria that survived through the purification steps to barcoding and library formation (SI Appendix, Fig. S4). Electron microscopy has revealed that mitochondria form close associations with nuclei in many kinds of cell, but particularly in ones that are metabolically and biosynthetically active or under stress (80). Such an intimate union between a nucleus and mitochondria initiates a process of interorganelle communication, known as retrograde signaling.

The pTGC have been inferred to be particularly vulnerable to xenobiotics and endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDC), such as bisphenol-A (BPA) acquired through maternal exposure (32). Among the outcomes are behavioral abnormalities in the pups. We have previously shown that developmental exposure to OXY reduced the thickness of the band of pTGC in the mid-pregnant placenta, as well as the area occupied by maternal blood vessels in the labyrinth, and a fall in the placental content of serotonin (39). The present study confirms the extensive loss of pTGC and presumed pTGC progenitors in the Cluster 1 nuclei that form a bridge with Cluster 10 (Figs. 1B and 6). Despite the pTGC deletion in response to OXY, pTGC do not express genes encoding recognized opioid receptors, although nuclei in areas of the UMAPs that might correspond to progenitors express low levels of transcripts for Oprm1 (SI Appendix, Fig. S6). We suggest that the direct placental targets for OXY are immature progenitors of Cluster 10 in Cluster 1, which then fail to mature. By contrast, the SpaTGC, which share many common features with pTGC (49, 67), appear not to be affected by developmental exposure to OXY. Neither do nuclei of the decidual cells and uterine epithelium contain significant levels of Oprm -k or- d-. Therefore, it seems unlikely that the action of OXY on the placenta is via the endometrium and indirect, although we cannot rule that out. Another more likely possibility is that the drug causes vasoconstriction of the maternal vessels that juxtapose the pTGC (59) and support their function. This would be consistent with the reduced diameter of maternal vessels previously noted in OXY-exposed placentas (39).

Accompanying the loss of Cluster 10 nuclei in response to OXY was the appearance of Cluster 14, which carried some pTGC markers but was notable for its striking display of transcripts encoding proteins implicated in responses to stress and toxic chemicals. Whether the cells providing Cluster 14 nuclei represent remnants from the pTGC lineage that arose as a direct response OXY exposure or an unusual placental cell type with a specialized role in responding to an environmental insult is unclear.

Finally, the transcriptome of E12.5 pTGC suggests that these cells display a strong genetic resemblance to human extravillous TB (Fig. 4A), a relationship previously proposed by others (49, 67). Their presence at the invasive front of the fetal placenta is also consistent with such a link. Whether there is a subset of human EVT that especially resemble mouse pTGC and whether they too are sensitive to a direct or indirect action of OXY is unknown. Our knowledge about the outcomes of opioid exposure on non-neuronal tissues, especially those of the placenta is limited, but the finding here, revealing that OXY can selectively lead to depletion of a prominent cell type in the mouse placenta, is a cautionary one for human health.

sec.title: Mouse OXY Treatments, Breeding, and Placenta Collections.
sec.p: Six- to eight-week-old female CD1 mice were treated daily with 5 mg/kg dose of oxycodone (Sigma, St. Louis, MO) or vehicle (0.9% saline solution, Moltox CAT # 51-40S022.052) control placed on a Nilla wafer (Nabisco Inc., Smithfield, RI), which they readily consume (32). This dose of OXY is identical to the one used in our previous studies and provides an approximation of the serum concentrations encountered in individuals consuming this drug (39). The mice began treatment two weeks prior to breeding and continued to receive the wafers through breeding until 12.5 d postconception. A total of three females were in each group. Two weeks following exposure to OXY or vehicle control, each female was paired in the late afternoon with an adult (8 to 10-wk-old) male CD 1 mouse. Each morning, the females were assessed for the presence of a copulatory plug. If none was observed, the males were removed temporarily and returned to the female partner that evening. The process was continued until all the females had been successfully bred. When a plug was observed, the female was moved to a separate cage, and the weight of the mouse was monitored for the next 12 d to confirm the pregnancy. The day a female exhibited a copulatory plug was considered embryonic age (E) 0.5.

At E 12.5 postconception, pregnant females were humanely euthanized by CO2 inhalation followed by cervical dislocation as based on the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) Guidelines for Euthanasia of Laboratory Mice, and both uterine horns dissected out. The uterine horns were maintained in 10 mL 1× PBS on ice to prevent the tissues from drying out during collection of individual placentas/decidual tissue. For placental and decidual tissue collection, each implantation site was separated from the uterus with fine-tipped forceps. The decidual tissue surrounding the placenta and conceptus was then gently pulled away and stored in a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The embryo and umbilical cord were carefully removed from the placenta, and the whole placenta placed in a second 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube before freezing. After collection, decidual and placental samples were moved from the liquid nitrogen to -80° C for storage until nuclei isolation.

sec.title: Nuclei Isolation and Library Preparation.
sec.p: Nuclei were isolated following a protocol detailed by Rousselle et al. (81) for human kidney biopsies, which we modified to suit mouse placental and decidual samples. Each sample was minced into roughly 1 mm pieces and returned to their original centrifuge tubes. A 7 mm micro stir-bar was placed in each tube, along with 1 mL lysis buffer that was composed of 1× PBS pH, 7.4 10 mM Tris–HCL pH 7.5,0.0125% Triton X-100, 1 mM dithiothreitol, and 0.2 U/mL RNAse inhibitor (Promega, Cat. No. PRN2611), and 1.5 μL DNAse I, RNase free (1 U/μL, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. AM2222). The samples were then placed on ice on a magnetic stir plate and stirred at ~350 RPM for 10 min. The contents were allowed to settle, and the supernatant solution removed by gentle suction with a P1000 pipette. The homogenate was passed through a 100 μm filter into a 15 mL collection tube and the filter washed with 6 mL nuclear wash and resuspension buffer (1× PBS, pH 7.4, 2 % bovine serum albumin [Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. A9418-50G], and 0.2 U/mL RNAse inhibitor). The process was repeated twice on the original tissue samples, and the three preparations combined, recentrifuged, resuspended, and filtered through a 100 μm filter. The pelleted nuclei were resuspended in 0.2 mL of ice-cold buffer and pipetted 50 times to minimize nuclear aggregation. Next, the isolated nuclei samples were transferred to a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube and were purified with OptiPrep as detailed in Martelotto’s protocol (82), which is recommended by Parse Biosciences. Isolated nuclei were fixed with Evercode™ Nuclei Fixation v2. Nuclei barcoding, cDNA synthesis, and library preparation were performed with the Parse Evercode™ WT v2 kit. SI Appendix, Fig. S7 illustrates the general experimental design for analyzing the placental and decidual tissue from mouse dams exposed to OXY or vehicle saline CTL with the Parse split-pool barcoding and snRNA-seq approach.

sec.title: Final Library Sequencing.
sec.p: The size and purity of the final library were determined with the Fragment Analyzer (Agilent Technologies, Inc.), quantified with the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay kit (Invitrogen), and diluted according to Illumina’s standard sequencing protocol. Libraries were pooled and run on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 sequencer by using a paired-end 100 bp read format on a S4 flow cell to generate ~100 million paired reads per sample. The actual number of reads is listed in SI Appendix, Table S2.

sec.title: snRNA-seq Data Processing.
sec.p: The raw single-nuclei RNA-Seq reads underwent preprocessing steps, including quality check, adapter trimming, and alignment to reference genome GRCm38 by using Parse Bioscience Pipeline (v1.0.6) (83). The count matrix was generated and analyzed in the package Seurat (v5.0.1) (84). Nuclei with fewer than 200 or greater than 12,500 unique genes, as well as nuclei from the A1 and A11 samples (Results), were excluded from final analyses. The counts were normalized and scaled by means of NormalizedData and ScaleData, respectively. PCA was performed by RunPCA, and the significant principal components (PCs) were assessed by ElbowPlot and DimHeatmap. The Dimensionality reduction and visualization of the UMAPs were performed by RunUMAP. We used the first 20 PCs for RunUMAP and FindNeighbors and set the resolution of FindClusters to 0.5.

sec.title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis (DGEA), TissueEnrich, PlacentaCellEnrich, WebGestalt, and g:Profiler.
sec.p: The FindAllMarkers function was used to determine the marker genes in each cluster relative to all other clusters. We performed differential expression analysis (DEA) comparing OXY vs. Saline Control conditions in both placenta and decidua tissues, as well as between placenta and decidua tissue. Genes were considered significantly regulated if fold change was ≥1, and adjusted P-value < 0.05. Differentially expressed transcripts in the different clusters were analyzed with the TissueEnrich program (47), PlacentaCellEnrich program (62), and WebGestalt to examine for mouse phenotype and ontology (65).

sec.title: Analysis of Spliced and Unspliced Matrices.
sec.p: Given that Seurat operates in R and available RNA Velocity packages are in Python, we exported the required data for RNA Velocity analysis. Using the provided Python scripts from Parse Bioscience Pipeline, we generated splice and unspliced matrices from their transcript assignment data file, which contains splicing information for each transcript, and converted the matrices into anndata object (85).
